definition: In statistics, the phi coefficient, also known as the mean square contingency coefficient or Yule coefficient of correlation and commonly denoted by φ or rφ, is a measure of association between two binary variables.
details: In machine learning and bioinformatics, it is known as the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). In meteorology and elsewhere, it is referred to as the Doolittle Measure of Association or Doolittle Skill Score. Described by Udny Yule in 1912 and given the name phi by Karl Pearson in the 1930s, it is a special case of the Pearson correlation coefficient.

explainer.lead: φ measures how strongly two yes/no variables are associated. It matters in ML because under the name Matthews correlation coefficient it gives a balanced quality score even when classes are very uneven.

tiers.eli5: It is a single number that tells you whether two yes/no questions tend to get the same answer, and how strongly.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers report MCC (φ) instead of accuracy on imbalanced classification tasks because it stays low when a model only predicts the majority class. Pitfall: it is unstable when a row or column of the contingency table is near zero.
tiers.paperLevel: φ = (n11·n00 − n10·n01) / sqrt((n11+n10)(n01+n00)(n11+n01)(n10+n00)), the Pearson correlation of two binary variables; it is bounded in [−1, 1] and undefined if any marginal is zero.

explainer.example: Predicting 40 true positives, 10 false positives, 20 false negatives and 30 true negatives gives φ = (40·30 − 10·20) / sqrt(50·50·60·40) ≈ 0.33.
